summary: Cedar Island Light at Cedar Point: an 1839 light, a granite tower of 1868, automated in 1934; county-owned, closed to visitors, and under restoration.

lens.where: USLHS: current optic moved to the breakwater; the 1855 sixth-order lens had been installed in the 1868 tower

structures.note: Square granite tower on a circular granite pier, 35 feet (10.7 m) from base to lantern centre (USLHS). Built under W. & G. Beattie of Fall River (LighthouseFriends).
L-shaped granite dwelling attached to the tower (USLHS: keepers' quarters 1868; LighthouseFriends).
The 1839 light was a one-and-a-half-story wooden keeper's dwelling with a small tower, replaced in 1868 (LighthouseFriends).

staffing.note: Automated light on a skeletal tower replaced the lighthouse in 1934 (LighthouseFriends; USLHS year discontinued 1934).

access.note: In Cedar Point County Park. Grounds open; dwelling and tower closed (LighthouseFriends). Restoration is under way, and no public access to the tower is yet in place (Dan's Papers, 2026; LI Parks, 2026).

facts.agency: Suffolk County (owner; Cedar Point County Park); Friends of the Cedar Island Lighthouse (501(c)(3) restoration group)

events.note: Congress provides $1,000 for a new light (LighthouseFriends)
Federal government buys Cedar Island from the town of East Hampton; another $2,500 from Congress (LighthouseFriends)
First light: a one-and-a-half-story keeper's dwelling with a small tower and nine Winslow Lewis lamps; USLHS gives 1839 as year established
Wooden keeper's dwelling with a small tower (LighthouseFriends)
Island about two acres; erosion halves it in under seventy years (LighthouseFriends)
Sixth-order Fresnel lens replaces the lamps and reflectors (USLHS and LighthouseFriends)
Dilapidated wooden structure struggles to support its cast-iron lantern (LighthouseFriends)
Congress approves $25,000 to rebuild the station (LighthouseFriends)
Granite tower and L-shaped dwelling built under W. & G. Beattie of Fall River; USLHS gives 1868 as tower established
The 1855 lens moves into the new tower, 44 feet above the water
Machine-operated fog bell added (LighthouseFriends)
Light-House Board report 1891-92, entry 186: boathouse moved and overhauled; drive well put down
Light-House Board report 1893-94, entry 208: set of boatways built
Light-House Board report for 1899, entry 246: set of fifth-order lamps furnished and fitted; various repairs
6,600 tons of rock added as riprap between 1903 and 1906 (LighthouseFriends)
13 July 1919: keeper William H. Follett takes three men burned in an explosion on the yacht Flyer to Sag Harbor; none of the three survived (Bulletin 1919; LighthouseFriends)
Automated light on a skeletal tower replaces the lighthouse; keeper Follett reassigned to Long Beach Bar Lighthouse (LighthouseFriends)
Year discontinued 1934 (USLHS)
Government puts the lighthouse up for sale; Phelan Beale buys it for $2,002 (LighthouseFriends)
Suffolk County purchases the property and adds it to Cedar Point County Park (LighthouseFriends gives 1967; the LI Parks news gives 1974)
Fire badly damages the empty building; interior destroyed; roof replaced, windows bricked over (LighthouseFriends; Friends of the Cedar Island Lighthouse)
NRIS record dated 18 April 2003. LighthouseFriends says 2002
1902 oil house restored (LighthouseFriends)
On 31 October 2013 the four-and-a-half-ton lantern room is lifted off and barged to Sag Harbor Yacht Yard (LighthouseFriends)
Lantern restored (Friends of the Cedar Island Lighthouse)
Suffolk County appropriates and the Legislature approves $300,000 for a new roof (Friends update, June 2016)
Suffolk County Legislature approves $500,000 for the roof, exterior and foundation pier (LighthouseFriends)
About $4 million appropriated as of fiscal 2023 for exterior preservation (Friends update, May 2024)
Suffolk County Environment, Parks and Agriculture Committee approves $1 million for the next phase: stabilization, interior stairwells, observation platforms (LI Parks, 5 March 2026)
Public ceremony for the lantern's return set for 1 August 2026 at Sag Harbor Yacht Club; lantern to be restored and reinstalled (Dan's Papers, 29 July 2026)

corrections.proposed: tower, granite, built 1868, 10.7 m (35 ft from base to lantern centre), standing
corrections.why: The 1839 light was a wooden dwelling with a small tower (LighthouseFriends). The present granite tower was built in 1868 (USLHS 'Year Tower Established: 1868', 'GRANITE'). The 10.7 m height matches the 1868 tower's 35 feet.
USLHS gives the light as 44 feet above water (about 13.4 m); LighthouseFriends says the 1855 lens shone 44 feet above the water in the 1868 tower. 7.6 m matches no source here.
The station's last keeper left in 1934 and an automated light replaced it that year (USLHS: year discontinued 1934; LighthouseFriends). No 1984 automation appears in any source here.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends says the National Register listing came in 2002. The NPGallery record (NRIS 03000248) gives 'Date Published' 4/18/2003, which is a publication date rather than a stated listing date. The story gives both dates with their sources.
LighthouseFriends calls the park both Cedar Point State Park and Cedar Point County Park; the 2026 sources (LI Parks; Dan's Papers) and the friends group say County Park, which the story uses.
LighthouseFriends describes the L-shaped dwelling as Victorian Gothic; the NRIS record lists the architectural style as Italianate. The story gives both.

notes_for_editor: The NRHP nomination is not digitised on NPGallery (its NPGallery record gives a file size of 22151 bytes, the same size as the Buffalo Main and Cedar Island records, so it appears to be a placeholder), so the nomination was not read. Wikipedia was not read. The LighthouseFriends anecdotes that have no primary source (Mulford's wooden legs, the grandsons' fish, the 1903 rabbit, the Bradley-era access dispute and the John Parker walk) are left out; the private owners are not named. The 1850 remark by a supply captain (Howland) is LighthouseFriends' quotation and is not verified against a Board report, so only its substance is used. The 1839 light's 'Fl G 4s' characteristic and 5.0 nm range in the record are not confirmed by any source read; the story does not use them. County acquisition date conflicts: LighthouseFriends 1967, LI Parks 1974; the story gives both. NRHP listing date conflicts: LighthouseFriends 2002, NRIS 18 April 2003; the NRIS date is used. The 1934 closure rests on the USLHS record and LighthouseFriends; no official report for 1934 was found in the corpus (Bulletin and Commissioner grep). The Bulletin 1919 OCR is poor, so evidence quotes use only the clean words; the rescue facts are read from the page image text. Chronicling America searches for 1930-1940 returned no pages (loc.gov HTTP 520, then zero hits). The Friends' .org domain returned 403; the .com pages were read. Current status: as of the Dan's Papers article (29 July 2026) the lantern was to return on 1 August 2026, and it is not confirmed whether it was reinstalled by 22 October 2026. The Light-House Board volume for 1899 is labelled by the corpus as 1899; the scan pages were taken from the corpus index. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the roster counts are 18 entries for 17 people (Fordham appears twice). The story now gives the NRIS style (Italianate) beside LighthouseFriends' Victorian Gothic, and the NRIS 'Date Published' (18 April 2003) beside LighthouseFriends' 2002. The 1919 Bulletin text is OCR: the names, the date and the 'power boat' and 'pleasure yacht' wording are read from the OCR text (the yacht's name is OCR'd as 'FlueI'' and is taken from LighthouseFriends, which also names the Flyer); the Bulletin is PDF page 35 (corpus.py page bulletin 1919). Report pages checked with corpus.py page: 1891-92 entry 186 at scan p.76; 1893-94 entry 208 at scan p.377; 1899 entry 246 at scan p.105. The Dan's Papers article of 29 July 2026 (cite 11) reports the Friends' statements; the story now attributes the restoration status to the article rather than to the Friends. The 'Congress' and 'Friends' statements are cited to the sources that make them.
